items.scene:
Narrator: We live in families. People in families help each other. They love each other, too. Not all families are the same. There are many kinds of families. Meet Seb. He's seven years old. Seb's family is big. He lives with his mother, father, three brothers, and two sisters.

Seb's family: We work together.

Narrator: This is Mandy. She's eight years old. She has one brother. They live with their grandmother and grandfather.

Mandy's family: We go places together.

Narrator: This is Kim. She's six years old. Her family is small. She lives with her mother.

Kim's family: We spend time together.

Narrator: Which family is like your family? Friends are also important. Friends have fun together, and they help each other, too. Seb, Mandy, and Kim are good friends. They go to school together. They play together every day.

Friends: We share things.

Narrator: Who are your good friends?
items.answer: Families can be different and still care for one another.
options: Families can be different and still care for one another.
items.hint: Look for the evidence. Listen again if you need to.
items.why: The opening explains that families love and help each other; the examples show different family sizes.

Narrator: We live in families. People in families help each other. They love each other, too. Not all families are the same. There are many kinds of families. Meet Seb. He's seven years old. Seb's family is big. He lives with his mother, father, three brothers, and two sisters.

Seb's family: We work together.

Narrator: This is Mandy. She's eight years old. She has one brother. They live with their grandmother and grandfather.

Mandy's family: We go places together.

Narrator: This is Kim. She's six years old. Her family is small. She lives with her mother.

Kim's family: We spend time together.

Narrator: Which family is like your family? Friends are also important. Friends have fun together, and they help each other, too. Seb, Mandy, and Kim are good friends. They go to school together. They play together every day.

Friends: We share things.

Narrator: Who are your good friends?

items.hint: Dùng is với he, she, it, một tên riêng hoặc một danh từ số ít. Dạng khẳng định có thể rút gọn thành he’s, she’s, it’s. Dạng phủ định “is not” có hai cách nói gọn: isn’t hoặc ’s not.
items.why: My mother is a teacher. Dùng is với he, she, it, một tên riêng hoặc một danh từ số ít. Dạng khẳng định có thể rút gọn thành he’s, she’s, it’s. Dạng phủ định “is not” có hai cách nói gọn: isn’t hoặc ’s not.

items.scene:
Narrator: We live in families. People in families help each other. They love each other, too. Not all families are the same. There are many kinds of families. Meet Seb. He's seven years old. Seb's family is big. He lives with his mother, father, three brothers, and two sisters.

Seb's family: We work together.

Narrator: This is Mandy. She's eight years old. She has one brother. They live with their grandmother and grandfather.

Mandy's family: We go places together.

Narrator: This is Kim. She's six years old. Her family is small. She lives with her mother.

Kim's family: We spend time together.

Narrator: Which family is like your family? Friends are also important. Friends have fun together, and they help each other, too. Seb, Mandy, and Kim are good friends. They go to school together. They play together every day.

Friends: We share things.

Narrator: Who are your good friends?
items.answer: Families can be different and still care for one another.
options: Families can be different and still care for one another.

items.scene:
Narrator: Elliot is a sad and lonely little elephant. He can't find his family. He walks and walks. He sees some tortoises.

Tuti: Hello, I'm Tuti. Who are you?

Elliot: I'm Elliot. I can't find my family.

Tuti: I can help. Let's go.

Narrator: They walk and walk. They see some zebras.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: No! Those are zebras. I'm not a zebra. I'm an elephant.

Narrator: The zebras see Elliot and Tuti. The zebras are scared and they run away. Tuti is Elliot's new friend. They eat together and they play together. Then they walk and walk again. They see some lions.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: No! Those are lions. I'm not a lion. I'm an elephant.

Narrator: The lions see Elliot and Tuti. Elliot and Tuti are scared and they run away. It's nighttime. They sleep side by side. The next day, they walk and walk again. They see some elephants.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: Yes! Those are elephants. I'm an elephant. Thank you, Tuti. You're my best friend.

Narrator: Now Elliot has a family and a friend.

items.scene:
Narrator: Elliot is a sad and lonely little elephant. He can't find his family. He walks and walks. He sees some tortoises.

Tuti: Hello, I'm Tuti. Who are you?

Elliot: I'm Elliot. I can't find my family.

Tuti: I can help. Let's go.

Narrator: They walk and walk. They see some zebras.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: No! Those are zebras. I'm not a zebra. I'm an elephant.

Narrator: The zebras see Elliot and Tuti. The zebras are scared and they run away. Tuti is Elliot's new friend. They eat together and they play together. Then they walk and walk again. They see some lions.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: No! Those are lions. I'm not a lion. I'm an elephant.

Narrator: The lions see Elliot and Tuti. Elliot and Tuti are scared and they run away. It's nighttime. They sleep side by side. The next day, they walk and walk again. They see some elephants.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: Yes! Those are elephants. I'm an elephant. Thank you, Tuti. You're my best friend.

Narrator: Now Elliot has a family and a friend.

items.scene:
Narrator: Elliot is a sad and lonely little elephant. He can't find his family. He walks and walks. He sees some tortoises.

Tuti: Hello, I'm Tuti. Who are you?

Elliot: I'm Elliot. I can't find my family.

Tuti: I can help. Let's go.

Narrator: They walk and walk. They see some zebras.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: No! Those are zebras. I'm not a zebra. I'm an elephant.

Narrator: The zebras see Elliot and Tuti. The zebras are scared and they run away. Tuti is Elliot's new friend. They eat together and they play together. Then they walk and walk again. They see some lions.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: No! Those are lions. I'm not a lion. I'm an elephant.

Narrator: The lions see Elliot and Tuti. Elliot and Tuti are scared and they run away. It's nighttime. They sleep side by side. The next day, they walk and walk again. They see some elephants.

Tuti: Is that your family?

Elliot: Yes! Those are elephants. I'm an elephant. Thank you, Tuti. You're my best friend.

Narrator: Now Elliot has a family and a friend.

Out in the garden Up in the tree There are four brown birds Can you see? Out in the garden Up in the tree There are three purple cats Can you see? Out in the garden Up in the tree There are two yellow dogs Can you see? Now there's a problem Look at the tree! There are twenty animals! Can you see? Roses are red, Spiders are black, Don't look now But there's one on your back! I like blue. I like the sky where birds fly high. I like yellow. I like the sun when we have fun. I like green. I like frogs as still as logs. I like black. I like the dark when foxes bark.

items.scene: There are three primary colors: red, blue, and yellow. There are three secondary colors: orange, purple, and green. We can mix primary colors to make secondary colors. The Color Wheel shows us primary and secondary colors. It also tells us how to make secondary colors. Look at orange. Red and yellow are the primary colors next to orange. We mix red and yellow to make orange. What primary colors are next to purple? Red and blue. We mix red and blue to make purple. The boys and girls paint a mural of the ocean at their school. In the mural there's yellow sand and there's a blue starfish. The starfish is under a seashell. And there's a big, red fish next to the seaweed. Can you see it? The children only have blue, red, and yellow paint. They want green, orange, and purple to finish their mural. They look at the Color Wheel and mix their paints to make these colors. Now there's green seaweed, an orange seashell, and lots of purple jellyfish. The mural is finished.

We mix red and yellow to make orange. What primary colors are next to purple? Red and blue. We mix red and blue to make purple. The boys and girls paint a mural of the ocean at their school. In the mural there's yellow sand and there's a blue starfish. The starfish is under a seashell. And there's a big, red fish next to the seaweed. Can you see it? The children only have blue, red, and yellow paint. They want green, orange, and purple to finish their mural. They look at the Color Wheel and mix their paints to make these colors. Now there's green seaweed, an orange seashell, and lots of purple jellyfish. The mural is finished.

items.scene: There are three primary colors: red, blue, and yellow. There are three secondary colors: orange, purple, and green. We can mix primary colors to make secondary colors. The Color Wheel shows us primary and secondary colors. It also tells us how to make secondary colors. Look at orange. Red and yellow are the primary colors next to orange. We mix red and yellow to make orange. What primary colors are next to purple? Red and blue. We mix red and blue to make purple. The boys and girls paint a mural of the ocean at their school. In the mural there's yellow sand and there's a blue starfish. The starfish is under a seashell. And there's a big, red fish next to the seaweed. Can you see it? The children only have blue, red, and yellow paint. They want green, orange, and purple to finish their mural. They look at the Color Wheel and mix their paints to make these colors. Now there's green seaweed, an orange seashell, and lots of purple jellyfish. The mural is finished.

items.storyText: There are three primary colors: red, blue, and yellow. There are three secondary colors: orange, purple, and green. We can mix primary colors to make secondary colors. The Color Wheel shows us primary and secondary colors. It also tells us how to make secondary colors. Look at orange. Red and yellow are the primary colors next to orange. We mix red and yellow to make orange. What primary colors are next to purple? Red and blue. We mix red and blue to make purple. The boys and girls paint a mural of the ocean at their school. In the mural there's yellow sand and there's a blue starfish. The starfish is under a seashell. And there's a big, red fish next to the seaweed. Can you see it? The children only have blue, red, and yellow paint. They want green, orange, and purple to finish their mural. They look at the Color Wheel and mix their paints to make these colors. Now there's green seaweed, an orange seashell, and lots of purple jellyfish. The mural is finished.

lessons.rawTitle: UNIT 5 – BEFORE YOU READ – READ – COMPREHENSION

items.scene: Animals make their homes in many places. Where are some animal homes? High in a tree is a big eagle's nest. There, eagles keep their chicks safe. Some eagles are white and brown. They eat rabbits, lizards, frogs, birds, and even small dogs! An opossum lives inside a tree hollow. It lines it with leaves and grass. Inside, it stays safe and dry. Opossums are gray or black. Mother opossums carry their babies on their backs. Honeybees make a hive for their home. They make honey in the hive. The bees have food all winter long. Honeybees have five eyes. Honeybees can't see the color red. Some crabs make their homes in old seashells. They find new seashells as they get big. Crabs live under water and on land. They have ten legs. An animal's home is the best place for it to live. Where is your home? How is your home right for you?

items.scene: Animals make their homes in many places. Where are some animal homes? High in a tree is a big eagle's nest. There, eagles keep their chicks safe. Some eagles are white and brown. They eat rabbits, lizards, frogs, birds, and even small dogs! An opossum lives inside a tree hollow. It lines it with leaves and grass. Inside, it stays safe and dry. Opossums are gray or black. Mother opossums carry their babies on their backs. Honeybees make a hive for their home. They make honey in the hive. The bees have food all winter long. Honeybees have five eyes. Honeybees can't see the color red. Some crabs make their homes in old seashells. They find new seashells as they get big. Crabs live under water and on land. They have ten legs. An animal's home is the best place for it to live. Where is your home? How is your home right for you?

items.scene: Animals make their homes in many places. Where are some animal homes? High in a tree is a big eagle's nest. There, eagles keep their chicks safe. Some eagles are white and brown. They eat rabbits, lizards, frogs, birds, and even small dogs! An opossum lives inside a tree hollow. It lines it with leaves and grass. Inside, it stays safe and dry. Opossums are gray or black. Mother opossums carry their babies on their backs. Honeybees make a hive for their home. They make honey in the hive. The bees have food all winter long. Honeybees have five eyes. Honeybees can't see the color red. Some crabs make their homes in old seashells. They find new seashells as they get big. Crabs live under water and on land. They have ten legs. An animal's home is the best place for it to live. Where is your home? How is your home right for you?

They eat rabbits, lizards, frogs, birds, and even small dogs! An opossum lives inside a tree hollow. It lines it with leaves and grass. Inside, it stays safe and dry. Opossums are gray or black. Mother opossums carry their babies on their backs. Honeybees make a hive for their home. They make honey in the hive. The bees have food all winter long. Honeybees have five eyes. Honeybees can't see the color red. Some crabs make their homes in old seashells. They find new seashells as they get big. Crabs live under water and on land. They have ten legs. An animal's home is the best place for it to live. Where is your home? How is your home right for you?

items.scene: Dian: This is a story about an orangutan called Anak, and how I teach her to live in the rainforest. My name is Dian. I take care of young orangutans at the Happy House Reserve. These young orangutans don't have families and can't live alone. The Happy House Reserve is in a rainforest. I teach the orangutans how to live in the rainforest. Anak is a baby. She lives at the reserve. I take care of her every day. I give her milk from a bottle. I teach Anak about the rainforest. We have fun together. Anak isn't sad or lonely. Anak is now four years old. She eats fruit, leaves, and flowers, and she can climb trees. She plays with her orangutan friends. But I am still Anak's special friend. Anak is eight years old now. She sleeps and eats at the reserve. I'm always happy to see her. She plays in the rainforest a lot. Sometimes she takes a nap there. I'm not with her in the rainforest. Anak is twelve years old now and she is very big. She lives and sleeps in the rainforest. I put out Anak's favorite foods, fruit and flowers, but she doesn't come. I miss Anak! Look! Who's this? It's Anak, and she has a baby! Anak and I are happy to see each other. I miss Anak every day, but I am happy. Anak can now live in the rainforest and teach her baby how to live there, too.

items.scene: Dian: This is a story about an orangutan called Anak, and how I teach her to live in the rainforest. My name is Dian. I take care of young orangutans at the Happy House Reserve. These young orangutans don't have families and can't live alone. The Happy House Reserve is in a rainforest. I teach the orangutans how to live in the rainforest. Anak is a baby. She lives at the reserve. I take care of her every day. I give her milk from a bottle. I teach Anak about the rainforest. We have fun together. Anak isn't sad or lonely. Anak is now four years old. She eats fruit, leaves, and flowers, and she can climb trees. She plays with her orangutan friends. But I am still Anak's special friend. Anak is eight years old now. She sleeps and eats at the reserve. I'm always happy to see her. She plays in the rainforest a lot. Sometimes she takes a nap there. I'm not with her in the rainforest. Anak is twelve years old now and she is very big. She lives and sleeps in the rainforest. I put out Anak's favorite foods, fruit and flowers, but she doesn't come. I miss Anak! Look! Who's this? It's Anak, and she has a baby! Anak and I are happy to see each other. I miss Anak every day, but I am happy. Anak can now live in the rainforest and teach her baby how to live there, too.

items.storyText: Dian: This is a story about an orangutan called Anak, and how I teach her to live in the rainforest. My name is Dian. I take care of young orangutans at the Happy House Reserve. These young orangutans don't have families and can't live alone. The Happy House Reserve is in a rainforest. I teach the orangutans how to live in the rainforest. Anak is a baby. She lives at the reserve. I take care of her every day. I give her milk from a bottle. I teach Anak about the rainforest. We have fun together. Anak isn't sad or lonely. Anak is now four years old. She eats fruit, leaves, and flowers, and she can climb trees. She plays with her orangutan friends. But I am still Anak's special friend. Anak is eight years old now. She sleeps and eats at the reserve. I'm always happy to see her. She plays in the rainforest a lot. Sometimes she takes a nap there. I'm not with her in the rainforest. Anak is twelve years old now and she is very big. She lives and sleeps in the rainforest. I put out Anak's favorite foods, fruit and flowers, but she doesn't come. I miss Anak! Look! Who's this? It's Anak, and she has a baby! Anak and I are happy to see each other. I miss Anak every day, but I am happy. Anak can now live in the rainforest and teach her baby how to live there, too.

items.scene: Dian: This is a story about an orangutan called Anak, and how I teach her to live in the rainforest. My name is Dian. I take care of young orangutans at the Happy House Reserve. These young orangutans don't have families and can't live alone. The Happy House Reserve is in a rainforest. I teach the orangutans how to live in the rainforest. Anak is a baby. She lives at the reserve. I take care of her every day. I give her milk from a bottle. I teach Anak about the rainforest. We have fun together. Anak isn't sad or lonely. Anak is now four years old. She eats fruit, leaves, and flowers, and she can climb trees. She plays with her orangutan friends. But I am still Anak's special friend. Anak is eight years old now. She sleeps and eats at the reserve. I'm always happy to see her. She plays in the rainforest a lot. Sometimes she takes a nap there. I'm not with her in the rainforest. Anak is twelve years old now and she is very big. She lives and sleeps in the rainforest. I put out Anak's favorite foods, fruit and flowers, but she doesn't come. I miss Anak! Look! Who's this? It's Anak, and she has a baby! Anak and I are happy to see each other. I miss Anak every day, but I am happy. Anak can now live in the rainforest and teach her baby how to live there, too.

items.scene: Dian: This is a story about an orangutan called Anak, and how I teach her to live in the rainforest. My name is Dian. I take care of young orangutans at the Happy House Reserve. These young orangutans don't have families and can't live alone. The Happy House Reserve is in a rainforest. I teach the orangutans how to live in the rainforest. Anak is a baby. She lives at the reserve. I take care of her every day. I give her milk from a bottle. I teach Anak about the rainforest. We have fun together. Anak isn't sad or lonely. Anak is now four years old. She eats fruit, leaves, and flowers, and she can climb trees. She plays with her orangutan friends. But I am still Anak's special friend. Anak is eight years old now. She sleeps and eats at the reserve. I'm always happy to see her. She plays in the rainforest a lot. Sometimes she takes a nap there. I'm not with her in the rainforest. Anak is twelve years old now and she is very big. She lives and sleeps in the rainforest. I put out Anak's favorite foods, fruit and flowers, but she doesn't come. I miss Anak! Look! Who's this? It's Anak, and she has a baby! Anak and I are happy to see each other. I miss Anak every day, but I am happy. Anak can now live in the rainforest and teach her baby how to live there, too.

items.scene: Dian: This is a story about an orangutan called Anak, and how I teach her to live in the rainforest. My name is Dian. I take care of young orangutans at the Happy House Reserve. These young orangutans don't have families and can't live alone. The Happy House Reserve is in a rainforest. I teach the orangutans how to live in the rainforest. Anak is a baby. She lives at the reserve. I take care of her every day. I give her milk from a bottle. I teach Anak about the rainforest. We have fun together. Anak isn't sad or lonely. Anak is now four years old. She eats fruit, leaves, and flowers, and she can climb trees. She plays with her orangutan friends. But I am still Anak's special friend. Anak is eight years old now. She sleeps and eats at the reserve. I'm always happy to see her. She plays in the rainforest a lot. Sometimes she takes a nap there. I'm not with her in the rainforest. Anak is twelve years old now and she is very big. She lives and sleeps in the rainforest. I put out Anak's favorite foods, fruit and flowers, but she doesn't come. I miss Anak! Look! Who's this? It's Anak, and she has a baby! Anak and I are happy to see each other. I miss Anak every day, but I am happy. Anak can now live in the rainforest and teach her baby how to live there, too.

items.scene: There are four seasons in a year: spring, summer, fall, and winter. Each season is special. Flowers and plants grow in spring. Summer days are long and hot. Fall leaves are beautiful colors. Winter days are short and cold. Spring is a growing season. It gets warm outside. It rains a lot. The rain helps plants grow. Buds grow on trees and plants. Birds make nests in trees. Summer comes after spring. It gets hot outside. The days are long and the nights are short. The sun helps the buds grow into fruit and flowers. Animals eat the fruit. Fall comes after summer. It gets cool outside. Leaves turn red, yellow, and orange. Then they fall to the ground. Animals collect food for the winter. Winter comes after fall. The days are short and the nights are long. It gets cold outside and it snows. The snow covers the ground. Lots of trees don't have leaves now. The animals eat the food they collect in the fall. Then it's spring, and the seasons begin again.

items.scene: There are four seasons in a year: spring, summer, fall, and winter. Each season is special. Flowers and plants grow in spring. Summer days are long and hot. Fall leaves are beautiful colors. Winter days are short and cold. Spring is a growing season. It gets warm outside. It rains a lot. The rain helps plants grow. Buds grow on trees and plants. Birds make nests in trees. Summer comes after spring. It gets hot outside. The days are long and the nights are short. The sun helps the buds grow into fruit and flowers. Animals eat the fruit. Fall comes after summer. It gets cool outside. Leaves turn red, yellow, and orange. Then they fall to the ground. Animals collect food for the winter. Winter comes after fall. The days are short and the nights are long. It gets cold outside and it snows. The snow covers the ground. Lots of trees don't have leaves now. The animals eat the food they collect in the fall. Then it's spring, and the seasons begin again.

lessons.rawTitle: UNIT 8 – BEFORE YOU READ – READ – COMPREHENSION

items.scene: Arnold: My name is Arnold. I have an apple tree. It keeps me busy all year. I watch small buds grow on my apple tree. They grow into apple blossoms. I watch honeybees collect nectar from the blossoms. I make a swing for my apple tree. I build a tree house in my apple tree. My apple tree shades me from the hot sun. I watch small apples begin to grow. I juggle some green apples for my tree friend. My apple tree now has big, red, tasty apples. I bring some leaves up to my tree house. I make a soft floor to lie on. I shake the branches. Red apples fall to the ground. I put them in a basket and take them home. My family and I make apple pies. In the winter, snow falls. It's quiet. The branches of my apple tree are bare. I hang strings of popcorn and berries on the branches. The birds eat them. I build a snowman. The snow melts. It's spring again.

items.storyTitle: The Seasons of Arnold's Apple Tree
items.storyText: Arnold: My name is Arnold. I have an apple tree. It keeps me busy all year. I watch small buds grow on my apple tree. They grow into apple blossoms. I watch honeybees collect nectar from the blossoms. I make a swing for my apple tree. I build a tree house in my apple tree. My apple tree shades me from the hot sun. I watch small apples begin to grow. I juggle some green apples for my tree friend. My apple tree now has big, red, tasty apples. I bring some leaves up to my tree house. I make a soft floor to lie on. I shake the branches. Red apples fall to the ground. I put them in a basket and take them home. My family and I make apple pies. In the winter, snow falls. It's quiet. The branches of my apple tree are bare. I hang strings of popcorn and berries on the branches. The birds eat them. I build a snowman. The snow melts. It's spring again.

items.scene: Arnold: My name is Arnold. I have an apple tree. It keeps me busy all year. I watch small buds grow on my apple tree. They grow into apple blossoms. I watch honeybees collect nectar from the blossoms. I make a swing for my apple tree. I build a tree house in my apple tree. My apple tree shades me from the hot sun. I watch small apples begin to grow. I juggle some green apples for my tree friend. My apple tree now has big, red, tasty apples. I bring some leaves up to my tree house. I make a soft floor to lie on. I shake the branches. Red apples fall to the ground. I put them in a basket and take them home. My family and I make apple pies. In the winter, snow falls. It's quiet. The branches of my apple tree are bare. I hang strings of popcorn and berries on the branches. The birds eat them. I build a snowman. The snow melts. It's spring again.

I watch small apples begin to grow. I juggle some green apples for my tree friend. My apple tree now has big, red, tasty apples. I bring some leaves up to my tree house. I make a soft floor to lie on. I shake the branches. Red apples fall to the ground. I put them in a basket and take them home. My family and I make apple pies. In the winter, snow falls. It's quiet. The branches of my apple tree are bare. I hang strings of popcorn and berries on the branches. The birds eat them. I build a snowman. The snow melts. It's spring again.

items.scene: Arnold: My name is Arnold. I have an apple tree. It keeps me busy all year. I watch small buds grow on my apple tree. They grow into apple blossoms. I watch honeybees collect nectar from the blossoms. I make a swing for my apple tree. I build a tree house in my apple tree. My apple tree shades me from the hot sun. I watch small apples begin to grow. I juggle some green apples for my tree friend. My apple tree now has big, red, tasty apples. I bring some leaves up to my tree house. I make a soft floor to lie on. I shake the branches. Red apples fall to the ground. I put them in a basket and take them home. My family and I make apple pies. In the winter, snow falls. It's quiet. The branches of my apple tree are bare. I hang strings of popcorn and berries on the branches. The birds eat them. I build a snowman. The snow melts. It's spring again.

items.scene: Look at the number line. It shows the numbers 1 to 20 in order. Some numbers are even and some numbers are odd. The even numbers are blue and the odd numbers are red. Read the even numbers aloud. When there are a lot of things in a group, we can use the even numbers to count the things by twos. This helps us to count fast. Count the fish by twos. We use addition every day. It helps us count things. We join groups of things with addition. This is a plus sign. It tells us to add the numbers together. This is an equals sign. It tells us that the numbers on both sides are the same amount. This is the answer. We say, “Two plus three equals five.” We write two plus sign three equals sign five. Let's use addition to work out answers to these word problems. You have eight orange seashells. I have nine green seashells. How many seashells do we have? Eight plus nine equals. They have six red crabs, five blue crabs, and four yellow crabs. How many crabs do they have? Six plus five plus four equals. How do you use addition every day?

items.scene: Look at the number line. It shows the numbers 1 to 20 in order. Some numbers are even and some numbers are odd. The even numbers are blue and the odd numbers are red. Read the even numbers aloud. When there are a lot of things in a group, we can use the even numbers to count the things by twos. This helps us to count fast. Count the fish by twos. We use addition every day. It helps us count things. We join groups of things with addition. This is a plus sign. It tells us to add the numbers together. This is an equals sign. It tells us that the numbers on both sides are the same amount. This is the answer. We say, “Two plus three equals five.” We write two plus sign three equals sign five. Let's use addition to work out answers to these word problems. You have eight orange seashells. I have nine green seashells. How many seashells do we have? Eight plus nine equals. They have six red crabs, five blue crabs, and four yellow crabs. How many crabs do they have? Six plus five plus four equals. How do you use addition every day?

items.scene:
Narrator: Hans and his wife, Ann, and their daughter, Olga, walk to a town. They see a woman.

Hans: We're very hungry, says Hans. Do you have any food?

Woman: No, says the woman. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: They see a man.

Olga: Olga says, We're hungry. Do you have any food?

Man: No, says the man. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: The family has a big pot. Hans puts water in it. Ann and Olga look for stones. They each find four stones and put them into the pot.

Woman and her friend: What's that? ask the woman and her friend.

Hans: It's stone soup, says Hans. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any potatoes. It's good with potatoes.

Woman: I have five! says the woman.

Woman's friend: I have seven, says her friend.

Narrator: They put the potatoes into the pot.

Man and his son: What's that? ask the man and his son.

Olga: It's stone soup, says Olga. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any sausages. It's good with sausages.

Man: I have two, says the man.

Son: I have three, says his son.

Narrator: They put the sausages into the pot. Later, the people from the town smell the soup and come out to look.

Townspeople: We have onions. We have carrots, they say, and put them into the pot.

Narrator: Everyone eats some soup.

Townspeople: We didn't have enough food, say the people. But we added our food together and now we all have tasty soup!

items.scene:
Narrator: Hans and his wife, Ann, and their daughter, Olga, walk to a town. They see a woman.

Hans: We're very hungry, says Hans. Do you have any food?

Woman: No, says the woman. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: They see a man.

Olga: Olga says, We're hungry. Do you have any food?

Man: No, says the man. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: The family has a big pot. Hans puts water in it. Ann and Olga look for stones. They each find four stones and put them into the pot.

Woman and her friend: What's that? ask the woman and her friend.

Hans: It's stone soup, says Hans. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any potatoes. It's good with potatoes.

Woman: I have five! says the woman.

Woman's friend: I have seven, says her friend.

Narrator: They put the potatoes into the pot.

Man and his son: What's that? ask the man and his son.

Olga: It's stone soup, says Olga. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any sausages. It's good with sausages.

Man: I have two, says the man.

Son: I have three, says his son.

Narrator: They put the sausages into the pot. Later, the people from the town smell the soup and come out to look.

Townspeople: We have onions. We have carrots, they say, and put them into the pot.

Narrator: Everyone eats some soup.

Townspeople: We didn't have enough food, say the people. But we added our food together and now we all have tasty soup!

items.scene:
Narrator: Hans and his wife, Ann, and their daughter, Olga, walk to a town. They see a woman.

Hans: We're very hungry, says Hans. Do you have any food?

Woman: No, says the woman. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: They see a man.

Olga: Olga says, We're hungry. Do you have any food?

Man: No, says the man. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: The family has a big pot. Hans puts water in it. Ann and Olga look for stones. They each find four stones and put them into the pot.

Woman and her friend: What's that? ask the woman and her friend.

Hans: It's stone soup, says Hans. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any potatoes. It's good with potatoes.

Woman: I have five! says the woman.

Woman's friend: I have seven, says her friend.

Narrator: They put the potatoes into the pot.

Man and his son: What's that? ask the man and his son.

Olga: It's stone soup, says Olga. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any sausages. It's good with sausages.

Man: I have two, says the man.

Son: I have three, says his son.

Narrator: They put the sausages into the pot. Later, the people from the town smell the soup and come out to look.

Townspeople: We have onions. We have carrots, they say, and put them into the pot.

Narrator: Everyone eats some soup.

Townspeople: We didn't have enough food, say the people. But we added our food together and now we all have tasty soup!

items.scene:
Narrator: Hans and his wife, Ann, and their daughter, Olga, walk to a town. They see a woman.

Hans: We're very hungry, says Hans. Do you have any food?

Woman: No, says the woman. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: They see a man.

Olga: Olga says, We're hungry. Do you have any food?

Man: No, says the man. I'm hungry, too!

Narrator: The family has a big pot. Hans puts water in it. Ann and Olga look for stones. They each find four stones and put them into the pot.

Woman and her friend: What's that? ask the woman and her friend.

Hans: It's stone soup, says Hans. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any potatoes. It's good with potatoes.

Woman: I have five! says the woman.

Woman's friend: I have seven, says her friend.

Narrator: They put the potatoes into the pot.

Man and his son: What's that? ask the man and his son.

Olga: It's stone soup, says Olga. It's tasty. You can try some, but we don't have any sausages. It's good with sausages.

Man: I have two, says the man.

Son: I have three, says his son.

Narrator: They put the sausages into the pot. Later, the people from the town smell the soup and come out to look.

Townspeople: We have onions. We have carrots, they say, and put them into the pot.

Narrator: Everyone eats some soup.

Townspeople: We didn't have enough food, say the people. But we added our food together and now we all have tasty soup!

items.scene:
Narrator: Tomas Flores is a farmer. He doesn't have a lot of money. He grows carrots, potatoes, and onions. He and his wife, Rosa, work hard every day. Farmer Flores has a cow. It gives lots of milk every day. Mrs. Flores sells the milk at the market in town. One day, Mrs. Flores comes home from town. She's very excited.

Mrs. Flores: There's a dance in town on Saturday. Can we go?

Farmer Flores: I'm sorry, but no, says Farmer Flores. We're plain people. It's too fancy for us!

Narrator: His wife is very sad. The next day, Farmer Flores has an idea. He takes the cow to town and sells it at the market. He buys a very fancy hat for himself and a beautiful dress for his wife. He runs home. He puts on the fancy hat. He gives his wife the beautiful dress.

Farmer Flores: We can go to the dance, he says.

Narrator: His wife is angry!

Mrs. Flores: Our cow gives us milk every day! she says. We sell the milk. We get money to buy food!

Farmer Flores: But you want beautiful clothes for the dance, says Farmer Flores.

Mrs. Flores: Can we eat the fancy hat and the beautiful dress? Mrs. Flores asks.

Farmer Flores: No, we can't, says the farmer. We need our cow!

Narrator: Farmer Flores takes the dress and the hat back to the market. He buys his cow back.

Farmer Flores: Now he tells people, Never sell something you need to buy something you want.

items.scene:
Narrator: Tomas Flores is a farmer. He doesn't have a lot of money. He grows carrots, potatoes, and onions. He and his wife, Rosa, work hard every day. Farmer Flores has a cow. It gives lots of milk every day. Mrs. Flores sells the milk at the market in town. One day, Mrs. Flores comes home from town. She's very excited.

Mrs. Flores: There's a dance in town on Saturday. Can we go?

Farmer Flores: I'm sorry, but no, says Farmer Flores. We're plain people. It's too fancy for us!

Narrator: His wife is very sad. The next day, Farmer Flores has an idea. He takes the cow to town and sells it at the market. He buys a very fancy hat for himself and a beautiful dress for his wife. He runs home. He puts on the fancy hat. He gives his wife the beautiful dress.

Farmer Flores: We can go to the dance, he says.

Narrator: His wife is angry!

Mrs. Flores: Our cow gives us milk every day! she says. We sell the milk. We get money to buy food!

Farmer Flores: But you want beautiful clothes for the dance, says Farmer Flores.

Mrs. Flores: Can we eat the fancy hat and the beautiful dress? Mrs. Flores asks.

Farmer Flores: No, we can't, says the farmer. We need our cow!

Narrator: Farmer Flores takes the dress and the hat back to the market. He buys his cow back.

Farmer Flores: Now he tells people, Never sell something you need to buy something you want.

items.scene: What do we want? Wants are things we would like to have. People want different things. Maria wants a kitten. Akif wants a new bicycle. What do we need? Needs are things we must have to live. People need the same things. We need a home to live in. We need food and water to grow and keep healthy. We need clothes to keep us warm. Needs are also things that are important to us and help us. Ji-Min needs a pencil to do her homework. Sam needs new sneakers to walk to school. We need money to buy the things we want and need. People have jobs to get money. Some people make or grow things to sell. A farmer grows food. A truck driver takes the food to the store. We go to the store to buy the food we need. Who do we need? Some people have service jobs. These are jobs that help other people get what they need. We need to learn, and to be safe and healthy. Police officers have a service job. They help us and keep us safe. Doctors have service jobs. They help keep us healthy. Teachers have service jobs, too. They help us learn. What other people have jobs that help us?
items.answer: Things we would like to have.

items.scene: What do we want? Wants are things we would like to have. People want different things. Maria wants a kitten. Akif wants a new bicycle. What do we need? Needs are things we must have to live. People need the same things. We need a home to live in. We need food and water to grow and keep healthy. We need clothes to keep us warm. Needs are also things that are important to us and help us. Ji-Min needs a pencil to do her homework. Sam needs new sneakers to walk to school. We need money to buy the things we want and need. People have jobs to get money. Some people make or grow things to sell. A farmer grows food. A truck driver takes the food to the store. We go to the store to buy the food we need. Who do we need? Some people have service jobs. These are jobs that help other people get what they need. We need to learn, and to be safe and healthy. Police officers have a service job. They help us and keep us safe. Doctors have service jobs. They help keep us healthy. Teachers have service jobs, too. They help us learn. What other people have jobs that help us?
items.answer: Things we would like to have.

items.scene: What do we want? Wants are things we would like to have. People want different things. Maria wants a kitten. Akif wants a new bicycle. What do we need? Needs are things we must have to live. People need the same things. We need a home to live in. We need food and water to grow and keep healthy. We need clothes to keep us warm. Needs are also things that are important to us and help us. Ji-Min needs a pencil to do her homework. Sam needs new sneakers to walk to school. We need money to buy the things we want and need. People have jobs to get money. Some people make or grow things to sell. A farmer grows food. A truck driver takes the food to the store. We go to the store to buy the food we need. Who do we need? Some people have service jobs. These are jobs that help other people get what they need. We need to learn, and to be safe and healthy. Police officers have a service job. They help us and keep us safe. Doctors have service jobs. They help keep us healthy. Teachers have service jobs, too. They help us learn. What other people have jobs that help us?
items.answer: Things we would like to have.

items.scene: The world is very big, and people live in all kinds of places. We all live in homes. Some homes are apartments. Some homes are houses. Some homes are big, and some homes are small. Homes are in neighborhoods. A neighborhood is where families live, work, and play. Some neighborhoods are in towns and cities, and some are in the country. Towns There are a lot of neighborhoods in towns. In towns there are parks, trees, and a lot of small streets. Many people live in houses. Some people live in apartments. This is Matias. Matias's house is in a town. I live in Loreto. Loreto is a small town. The Country In the country there are woods, farms, and fields. Many people live on farms. People live in houses, too. There are no apartment buildings. Houses in the country are far apart. This is Jenna's house. I live on a farm in the country. Cities Cities are like very big towns. There are a lot of people, streets, and big buildings in cities. The buildings are close together. Many people live in apartments. This is Nada. Nada's apartment is in the city. I live in Cairo. Cairo is a big city. What's your address? Everyone's home has an address. It tells us where it is. My address is 19 Main Street, Rivertown. When do we use an address? We write an address on a letter. We use an address to find our friend's house. What's your address?

Towns There are a lot of neighborhoods in towns. In towns there are parks, trees, and a lot of small streets. Many people live in houses. Some people live in apartments. This is Matias. Matias's house is in a town. I live in Loreto. Loreto is a small town. The Country In the country there are woods, farms, and fields. Many people live on farms. People live in houses, too. There are no apartment buildings. Houses in the country are far apart. This is Jenna's house. I live on a farm in the country. Cities Cities are like very big towns. There are a lot of people, streets, and big buildings in cities. The buildings are close together. Many people live in apartments. This is Nada. Nada's apartment is in the city. I live in Cairo. Cairo is a big city. What's your address? Everyone's home has an address. It tells us where it is. My address is 19 Main Street, Rivertown. When do we use an address? We write an address on a letter. We use an address to find our friend's house. What's your address?

items.scene: The world is very big, and people live in all kinds of places. We all live in homes. Some homes are apartments. Some homes are houses. Some homes are big, and some homes are small. Homes are in neighborhoods. A neighborhood is where families live, work, and play. Some neighborhoods are in towns and cities, and some are in the country. Towns There are a lot of neighborhoods in towns. In towns there are parks, trees, and a lot of small streets. Many people live in houses. Some people live in apartments. This is Matias. Matias's house is in a town. I live in Loreto. Loreto is a small town. The Country In the country there are woods, farms, and fields. Many people live on farms. People live in houses, too. There are no apartment buildings. Houses in the country are far apart. This is Jenna's house. I live on a farm in the country. Cities Cities are like very big towns. There are a lot of people, streets, and big buildings in cities. The buildings are close together. Many people live in apartments. This is Nada. Nada's apartment is in the city. I live in Cairo. Cairo is a big city. What's your address? Everyone's home has an address. It tells us where it is. My address is 19 Main Street, Rivertown. When do we use an address? We write an address on a letter. We use an address to find our friend's house. What's your address?

Homes are in neighborhoods. A neighborhood is where families live, work, and play. Some neighborhoods are in towns and cities, and some are in the country. Towns There are a lot of neighborhoods in towns. In towns there are parks, trees, and a lot of small streets. Many people live in houses. Some people live in apartments. This is Matias. Matias's house is in a town. I live in Loreto. Loreto is a small town. The Country In the country there are woods, farms, and fields. Many people live on farms. People live in houses, too. There are no apartment buildings. Houses in the country are far apart. This is Jenna's house. I live on a farm in the country. Cities Cities are like very big towns. There are a lot of people, streets, and big buildings in cities. The buildings are close together. Many people live in apartments. This is Nada. Nada's apartment is in the city. I live in Cairo. Cairo is a big city. What's your address? Everyone's home has an address. It tells us where it is. My address is 19 Main Street, Rivertown. When do we use an address? We write an address on a letter. We use an address to find our friend's house. What's your address?

items.scene:
Narrator: City Mouse lives in the city.

City Mouse: There are too many people and cars here. I want some fresh air! I can visit my cousin, Country Mouse, he says.

Narrator: City Mouse flies to the country. Country Mouse runs to him.

Country Mouse: Hello, City Mouse! Welcome to my home!

City Mouse: Thanks, Country Mouse! says City Mouse. I'm hungry. What's for dinner?

Narrator: They go to the cornfield and eat some corn. Then they go to the orchard and eat some apples.

City Mouse: This food is okay, but it's too plain for me! says City Mouse.

Narrator: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in an old barn. The next morning, they walk to the pond.

City Mouse: The country is okay, but it's too boring for me, says City Mouse. Come with me to the city! It's interesting there.

Country Mouse: OK, says Country Mouse.

Narrator: City Mouse and Country Mouse take a train to the city. They go to a movie theater, a department store, and a restaurant. They eat cheese and cookies.

Country Mouse: This food is okay, but it's too fancy for me, says Country Mouse.

Narrator: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in a new hotel. The next morning, they hear a loud noise.

City Mouse: Cats! Run! says City Mouse.

Narrator: City Mouse and Country Mouse run and run until they are safe.

Country Mouse: The city is okay, but it's too dangerous for me! says Country Mouse. Come with me to the country. It's safe there.

City Mouse: No, the country is good for you, and the city is good for me, says City Mouse.

Narrator: The two mice say goodbye and go home happy.

items.scene:
Narrator: City Mouse lives in the city.

City Mouse: There are too many people and cars here. I want some fresh air! I can visit my cousin, Country Mouse, he says.

Narrator: City Mouse flies to the country. Country Mouse runs to him.

Country Mouse: Hello, City Mouse! Welcome to my home!

City Mouse: Thanks, Country Mouse! says City Mouse. I'm hungry. What's for dinner?

Narrator: They go to the cornfield and eat some corn. Then they go to the orchard and eat some apples.

City Mouse: This food is okay, but it's too plain for me! says City Mouse.

Narrator: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in an old barn. The next morning, they walk to the pond.

City Mouse: The country is okay, but it's too boring for me, says City Mouse. Come with me to the city! It's interesting there.

Country Mouse: OK, says Country Mouse.

Narrator: City Mouse and Country Mouse take a train to the city. They go to a movie theater, a department store, and a restaurant. They eat cheese and cookies.

Country Mouse: This food is okay, but it's too fancy for me, says Country Mouse.

Narrator: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in a new hotel. The next morning, they hear a loud noise.

City Mouse: Cats! Run! says City Mouse.

Narrator: City Mouse and Country Mouse run and run until they are safe.

Country Mouse: The city is okay, but it's too dangerous for me! says Country Mouse. Come with me to the country. It's safe there.

City Mouse: No, the country is good for you, and the city is good for me, says City Mouse.

Narrator: The two mice say goodbye and go home happy.

dialogue.speaker: City Mouse
dialogue.text: There are too many people and cars here. I want some fresh air! I can visit my cousin, Country Mouse, he says.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: City Mouse flies to the country. Country Mouse runs to him.

dialogue.speaker: Country Mouse
dialogue.text: Hello, City Mouse! Welcome to my home!

dialogue.speaker: City Mouse
dialogue.text: Thanks, Country Mouse! says City Mouse. I'm hungry. What's for dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: They go to the cornfield and eat some corn. Then they go to the orchard and eat some apples.

dialogue.speaker: City Mouse
dialogue.text: This food is okay, but it's too plain for me! says City Mouse.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in an old barn. The next morning, they walk to the pond.

dialogue.speaker: City Mouse
dialogue.text: The country is okay, but it's too boring for me, says City Mouse. Come with me to the city! It's interesting there.

dialogue.speaker: Country Mouse
dialogue.text: OK, says Country Mouse.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: City Mouse and Country Mouse take a train to the city. They go to a movie theater, a department store, and a restaurant. They eat cheese and cookies.

dialogue.speaker: Country Mouse
dialogue.text: This food is okay, but it's too fancy for me, says Country Mouse.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in a new hotel. The next morning, they hear a loud noise.

dialogue.speaker: City Mouse
dialogue.text: Cats! Run! says City Mouse.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: City Mouse and Country Mouse run and run until they are safe.

dialogue.speaker: Country Mouse
dialogue.text: The city is okay, but it's too dangerous for me! says Country Mouse. Come with me to the country. It's safe there.

dialogue.speaker: City Mouse
dialogue.text: No, the country is good for you, and the city is good for me, says City Mouse.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.text: The two mice say goodbye and go home happy.

items.scene:
Narrator: City Mouse lives in the city.

City Mouse: There are too many people and cars here. I want some fresh air! I can visit my cousin, Country Mouse, he says.

Narrator: City Mouse flies to the country. Country Mouse runs to him.

Country Mouse: Hello, City Mouse! Welcome to my home!

City Mouse: Thanks, Country Mouse! says City Mouse. I'm hungry. What's for dinner?

Narrator: They go to the cornfield and eat some corn. Then they go to the orchard and eat some apples.

City Mouse: This food is okay, but it's too plain for me! says City Mouse.

Narrator: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in an old barn. The next morning, they walk to the pond.

City Mouse: The country is okay, but it's too boring for me, says City Mouse. Come with me to the city! It's interesting there.

Country Mouse: OK, says Country Mouse.

Narrator: City Mouse and Country Mouse take a train to the city. They go to a movie theater, a department store, and a restaurant. They eat cheese and cookies.

Country Mouse: This food is okay, but it's too fancy for me, says Country Mouse.

Narrator: It's bedtime and they're tired. They sleep in a new hotel. The next morning, they hear a loud noise.

City Mouse: Cats! Run! says City Mouse.

Narrator: City Mouse and Country Mouse run and run until they are safe.

Country Mouse: The city is okay, but it's too dangerous for me! says Country Mouse. Come with me to the country. It's safe there.

City Mouse: No, the country is good for you, and the city is good for me, says City Mouse.

Narrator: The two mice say goodbye and go home happy.

lessons.rawTitle: UNIT 15 – BEFORE YOU READ – READ – COMPREHENSION

items.scene: Percussion instruments are a family of musical instruments. We strike or shake them. Percussion instruments are big and small. These instruments add special sounds to music. Percussion instruments keep the beat: 1, 2, 3, 4. We can keep the beat, too. Clap your hands to this beat: 1, 2, 3, 4. Can you stamp your feet to the beat? 1, 2, 3, 4. items.scene: Percussion instruments are a family of musical instruments. We strike or shake them. Percussion instruments are big and small. These instruments add special sounds to music. Percussion instruments keep the beat: 1, 2, 3, 4. We can keep the beat, too. Clap your hands to this beat: 1, 2, 3, 4. Can you stamp your feet to the beat? 1, 2, 3, 4. Drums There are a lot of different drums in the world. We strike drums with our fingers, our hands, or with drumsticks or mallets. This keeps the beat. This big drum is called a bass drum. The boy is striking the big white drum with two mallets. The Tambourine A tambourine is like a small drum. We strike it with our hands. We can shake it, too. The Xylophone A xylophone has wooden bars. The girl is striking the xylophone with mallets. The Triangle Why do you think this instrument is called a triangle? Its shape is a triangle. We strike it. Cymbals When we play the cymbals, we strike two cymbals together. There are many kinds of cymbals. Some are big and some are small. They sound different. This boy is playing big cymbals. Listen. They're playing all the percussion instruments again. Which instrument is your favorite?

items.scene: Maddie: January I'm Maddie and we're students in Ms. King's class. We want music lessons, but we don't have instruments. We can't buy instruments because we don't have any money. We have a big problem. We need a good idea. February We think, and think, and think, and then get an idea. Let's make instruments and give a concert! We can sell tickets, get money, and buy new instruments. But how do we make instruments? We ask our friends and families. Aha! We can use things from our homes. April We're making instruments that we can shake. We're using paper rolls and beads. Fay and Oscar are shaking them. Evan and Kate are using jars and candy. They're shaking them to a beat. May We're all practicing our instruments. These buckets and pots are our drums. Bruno, Sara, and Dan are striking them. These are our cymbals. Aziz and I are striking them together. Ms. King is helping us. What do you think? Are we having fun? June It's concert night. Look at all the people! They're buying tickets. Everyone is excited. We're all playing our instruments, singing, and dancing. Our parents are taking pictures. The people are clapping and giving money! It's a wonderful concert. September Look! These are our new instruments! We're very happy. We're playing them and we sound great. We still like our old instruments, too!

items.scene: Maddie: January I'm Maddie and we're students in Ms. King's class. We want music lessons, but we don't have instruments. We can't buy instruments because we don't have any money. We have a big problem. We need a good idea. February We think, and think, and think, and then get an idea. Let's make instruments and give a concert! We can sell tickets, get money, and buy new instruments. But how do we make instruments? We ask our friends and families. Aha! We can use things from our homes. April We're making instruments that we can shake. We're using paper rolls and beads. Fay and Oscar are shaking them. Evan and Kate are using jars and candy. They're shaking them to a beat. May We're all practicing our instruments. These buckets and pots are our drums. Bruno, Sara, and Dan are striking them. These are our cymbals. Aziz and I are striking them together. Ms. King is helping us. What do you think? Are we having fun? June It's concert night. Look at all the people! They're buying tickets. Everyone is excited. We're all playing our instruments, singing, and dancing. Our parents are taking pictures. The people are clapping and giving money! It's a wonderful concert. September Look! These are our new instruments! We're very happy. We're playing them and we sound great. We still like our old instruments, too!

items.scene: Maddie: January I'm Maddie and we're students in Ms. King's class. We want music lessons, but we don't have instruments. We can't buy instruments because we don't have any money. We have a big problem. We need a good idea. February We think, and think, and think, and then get an idea. Let's make instruments and give a concert! We can sell tickets, get money, and buy new instruments. But how do we make instruments? We ask our friends and families. Aha! We can use things from our homes. April We're making instruments that we can shake. We're using paper rolls and beads. Fay and Oscar are shaking them. Evan and Kate are using jars and candy. They're shaking them to a beat. May We're all practicing our instruments. These buckets and pots are our drums. Bruno, Sara, and Dan are striking them. These are our cymbals. Aziz and I are striking them together. Ms. King is helping us. What do you think? Are we having fun? June It's concert night. Look at all the people! They're buying tickets. Everyone is excited. We're all playing our instruments, singing, and dancing. Our parents are taking pictures. The people are clapping and giving money! It's a wonderful concert. September Look! These are our new instruments! We're very happy. We're playing them and we sound great. We still like our old instruments, too!

We have a big problem. We need a good idea. February We think, and think, and think, and then get an idea. Let's make instruments and give a concert! We can sell tickets, get money, and buy new instruments. But how do we make instruments? We ask our friends and families. Aha! We can use things from our homes. April We're making instruments that we can shake. We're using paper rolls and beads. Fay and Oscar are shaking them. Evan and Kate are using jars and candy. They're shaking them to a beat. May We're all practicing our instruments. These buckets and pots are our drums. Bruno, Sara, and Dan are striking them. These are our cymbals. Aziz and I are striking them together. Ms. King is helping us. What do you think? Are we having fun? June It's concert night. Look at all the people! They're buying tickets. Everyone is excited. We're all playing our instruments, singing, and dancing. Our parents are taking pictures. The people are clapping and giving money! It's a wonderful concert. September Look! These are our new instruments! We're very happy. We're playing them and we sound great. We still like our old instruments, too!

lessons.rawTitle: UNIT 17 – BEFORE YOU READ – READ – COMPREHENSION

items.scene: We see many things in our world every day. All of these things are living or nonliving. Let's read about how they are different. Living things A living thing can grow and change. Look at the caterpillar and butterfly. What is different? A plant is a living thing. An animal is a living thing. You are a living thing! Living things breathe air and they need food and water. People and animals can move by themselves. They can get food and water from different places. Where can animals get water? Plants can't move by themselves. They make their food from sunlight, water, and air. They can grow tall to get sunlight. Water comes to them. What living things do you see every day? Nonliving things A nonliving thing doesn't need food, air, or water. It can't breathe. A toy is a nonliving thing. A nonliving thing doesn't grow, but it can change. Look at the sneakers. What's different? A ball can move. Is a ball a living thing? No, it isn't. A ball can only move if we move it. It can't move by itself. It can't breathe and it doesn't grow. It's a nonliving thing. What nonliving things do you move every day? Look around you. What nonliving things do you see? All living and nonliving things in our world are important. It is good to take care of all of them.

items.scene: We see many things in our world every day. All of these things are living or nonliving. Let's read about how they are different. Living things A living thing can grow and change. Look at the caterpillar and butterfly. What is different? A plant is a living thing. An animal is a living thing. You are a living thing! Living things breathe air and they need food and water. People and animals can move by themselves. They can get food and water from different places. Where can animals get water? Plants can't move by themselves. They make their food from sunlight, water, and air. They can grow tall to get sunlight. Water comes to them. What living things do you see every day? Nonliving things A nonliving thing doesn't need food, air, or water. It can't breathe. A toy is a nonliving thing. A nonliving thing doesn't grow, but it can change. Look at the sneakers. What's different? A ball can move. Is a ball a living thing? No, it isn't. A ball can only move if we move it. It can't move by itself. It can't breathe and it doesn't grow. It's a nonliving thing. What nonliving things do you move every day? Look around you. What nonliving things do you see? All living and nonliving things in our world are important. It is good to take care of all of them.

What nonliving things do you move every day? Look around you. What nonliving things do you see? All living and nonliving things in our world are important. It is good to take care of all of them.

items.scene:
Narrator: One day, an old woman makes a gingerbread man cookie. She bakes it in the oven.

Old woman: It smells good! I'm hungry!

Narrator: The old woman opens the oven door. The gingerbread man jumps up and runs out the door!

Old woman and old man: Stop! Don't run away! We want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman and old man chase the gingerbread man. He should run fast!

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: The gingerbread man sees a chicken in the yard.

Chicken: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, and the chicken all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: He sees a cow in a grassy field.

Cow: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, chicken, and the cow all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: He sees a horse next to a tree.

Horse: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, chicken, cow, and the horse all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: The gingerbread man comes to a river. He should swim across it!

Gingerbread Man: Oh, no! I can't swim!

Narrator: The gingerbread man sees a fox. He shouldn't talk to the fox!

Fox: You really shouldn't stay here. I can help you. Climb on my nose and we can cross the river.

Gingerbread Man: OK!

Narrator: The gingerbread man jumps on the fox's nose. The fox throws the gingerbread man up in the air and ...

Fox: Yum! Delicious!

Narrator: And that's the end of the gingerbread man!

items.storyText:
Narrator: One day, an old woman makes a gingerbread man cookie. She bakes it in the oven.

Old woman: It smells good! I'm hungry!

Narrator: The old woman opens the oven door. The gingerbread man jumps up and runs out the door!

Old woman and old man: Stop! Don't run away! We want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman and old man chase the gingerbread man. He should run fast!

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: The gingerbread man sees a chicken in the yard.

Chicken: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, and the chicken all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: He sees a cow in a grassy field.

Cow: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, chicken, and the cow all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: He sees a horse next to a tree.

Horse: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, chicken, cow, and the horse all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: The gingerbread man comes to a river. He should swim across it!

Gingerbread Man: Oh, no! I can't swim!

Narrator: The gingerbread man sees a fox. He shouldn't talk to the fox!

Fox: You really shouldn't stay here. I can help you. Climb on my nose and we can cross the river.

Gingerbread Man: OK!

Narrator: The gingerbread man jumps on the fox's nose. The fox throws the gingerbread man up in the air and ...

Fox: Yum! Delicious!

Narrator: And that's the end of the gingerbread man!

items.scene:
Narrator: One day, an old woman makes a gingerbread man cookie. She bakes it in the oven.

Old woman: It smells good! I'm hungry!

Narrator: The old woman opens the oven door. The gingerbread man jumps up and runs out the door!

Old woman and old man: Stop! Don't run away! We want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman and old man chase the gingerbread man. He should run fast!

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: The gingerbread man sees a chicken in the yard.

Chicken: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, and the chicken all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: He sees a cow in a grassy field.

Cow: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, chicken, and the cow all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: He sees a horse next to a tree.

Horse: Stop! Don't run away! I want to eat you!

Narrator: The old woman, old man, chicken, cow, and the horse all chase the gingerbread man. But he's too fast.

Gingerbread Man: Run, run as fast as you can! You can't catch me, I'm the gingerbread man!

Narrator: The gingerbread man comes to a river. He should swim across it!

Gingerbread Man: Oh, no! I can't swim!

Narrator: The gingerbread man sees a fox. He shouldn't talk to the fox!

Fox: You really shouldn't stay here. I can help you. Climb on my nose and we can cross the river.

Gingerbread Man: OK!

Narrator: The gingerbread man jumps on the fox's nose. The fox throws the gingerbread man up in the air and ...

Fox: Yum! Delicious!

Narrator: And that's the end of the gingerbread man!
